q: Which agency is the lead agency in the enforcement of the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002?
a: Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA)
Philippine National Police (PNP)
National Bureau of Investigation (NBI)
Dangerous Drugs Board (DDB)
r: Section 82 of R.A. 9165 created PDEA as the implementing arm and lead agency against illegal drugs.
The PNP keeps an anti-drug unit, but it acts under the coordination of PDEA, not as the lead agency.
The NBI may investigate drug cases, but R.A. 9165 makes PDEA the lead enforcement agency.
The DDB is the policy-making and strategy-formulating body; it does not lead enforcement.
e: R.A. 9165 separates policy (Dangerous Drugs Board) from enforcement, and names PDEA the lead agency in enforcing the law.

q: Why is the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) counted as a law enforcement agency in the criminal justice system?
a: It enforces the Fire Code and investigates the cause of fires, including arson
It prosecutes arson cases in court on behalf of the people
It decides administrative cases filed against police officers
It keeps custody of persons convicted of destructive arson
r: Besides fire suppression, the BFP enforces fire safety laws and conducts fire and arson investigations that support criminal cases.
Prosecution of crimes belongs to the public prosecutor, not to the BFP.
Administrative cases against police officers are handled by bodies such as NAPOLCOM, IAS and PLEB.
Custody of convicted persons is a function of the correction pillar (BuCor, BJMP, provincial jails).
e: The BFP belongs to the law enforcement pillar because it enforces the Fire Code and investigates fires and arson.
l: R.A. 6975; R.A. 9514 (Fire Code of the Philippines)

q: During an inquest, what is the main task of the inquest prosecutor?
a: To determine whether a person arrested without a warrant should be charged and kept in custody
To decide whether the arrested person is guilty beyond reasonable doubt
To issue a warrant of arrest against the person arrested
To conduct the arraignment and receive the plea of the accused
r: An inquest is a summary inquiry by the prosecutor into a warrantless arrest to decide whether the person should be charged in court and remain detained.
Guilt beyond reasonable doubt is decided by the court after trial, not by the prosecutor.
Warrants of arrest are issued only by judges.
Arraignment takes place in court after the information has been filed.
e: Inquest applies to warrantless arrests; preliminary investigation, by contrast, is a fuller inquiry into probable cause when the respondent is not under lawful arrest.
l: Rule 112, Rules of Criminal Procedure; DOJ rules on inquest

q: An offense is punishable by imprisonment of up to four years. Which court has exclusive original jurisdiction over it?
a: Municipal or Metropolitan Trial Court
Regional Trial Court (second-level court)
Court of Appeals
Sandiganbayan
r: First-level courts try offenses punishable by imprisonment not exceeding six years, regardless of the fine.
The RTC tries offenses punishable by imprisonment exceeding six years.
The Court of Appeals is an appellate court; it does not try such offenses originally.
The Sandiganbayan hears graft and related cases of certain high-ranking public officers.
e: Under B.P. 129 as amended by R.A. 7691, offenses punishable by imprisonment of not more than six years fall within first-level courts.
l: B.P. 129, Sec. 32, as amended by R.A. 7691

q: How do the BJMP and the BuCor differ in the criminal justice system?
a: BJMP runs district, city and municipal jails; BuCor runs the national penitentiaries
BJMP runs the national penitentiaries; BuCor runs the city and municipal jails
BJMP supervises probationers; BuCor supervises parolees
BJMP is under the DOJ; BuCor is under the DILG
r: The BJMP manages district, city and municipal jails, while BuCor keeps national (insular) prisoners in the penitentiaries.
This reverses the two agencies' mandates.
Probationers and parolees are supervised by the Probation and Parole Administration.
It is the other way around: the BJMP is under the DILG and BuCor is under the DOJ.
e: Both belong to the correction pillar, but at different levels: the BJMP for local jails and BuCor for national prisoners sentenced to more than three years.

q: A city ordinance imposes a curfew on all minors but exempts minors who are working students. Under which test is this classification judged against the equal protection clause?
a: Whether it rests on substantial distinctions germane to the purpose of the law
Whether it gives every resident exactly the same treatment
Whether the minors were given notice and a hearing before it was passed
Whether it was approved by the President before it took effect
r: Equal protection allows classification if it rests on substantial distinctions, is germane to the law's purpose, is not limited to existing conditions, and applies equally to all members of the class.
Equal protection does not require identical treatment of everyone; reasonable classification is allowed.
Notice and hearing is the test of procedural due process, not of equal protection.
Presidential approval has nothing to do with the validity of a city ordinance under equal protection.
e: Due process asks whether the law and the procedure are fair; equal protection asks whether persons are classified on reasonable grounds.

q: A suspect is brought to the station and investigators begin asking him about a robbery. What must they do first?
a: Inform him of his right to remain silent and to have competent and independent counsel
Ask him to sign a waiver of his rights before any counsel arrives
Take his sworn statement first and call a lawyer once he has confessed
Allow only his immediate family to visit him after the investigation ends
r: Before custodial investigation begins, the person must be informed in a language he understands of his right to remain silent and to counsel.
A waiver of these rights is valid only if made in writing and in the presence of counsel.
A confession taken without counsel is inadmissible.
R.A. 7438 lets the family, a doctor or a priest visit him at any time during custodial investigation, not only after it ends.
e: R.A. 7438 and the Constitution protect the person under custodial investigation; violating these rights makes the confession inadmissible and exposes the officer to liability.

q: Police officers without a warrant search a house because a neighbor said drugs might be inside. No one in the house consented. What is the status of the drugs they seized?
a: Inadmissible, because the warrantless search was unreasonable
Admissible, because the neighbor gave reliable information
Admissible, because drugs are contraband and may always be seized
Inadmissible only if the owner later pays the court fees
r: A search of a home without a warrant, consent or any recognized exception violates Art. III, Sec. 2, and its fruits are inadmissible under Sec. 3(2).
A tip alone does not replace a search warrant issued by a judge.
Contraband found in plain view during a lawful intrusion may be seized, but this search was not lawful to begin with.
Admissibility does not depend on the payment of court fees.
e: The exclusionary rule bars evidence obtained in violation of the right against unreasonable searches and seizures.

q: An accused objects to giving his fingerprints, saying it violates his right against self-incrimination. Is his objection correct?
a: No, because the right covers only testimonial compulsion, not physical evidence
Yes, because the right covers every kind of evidence taken from the accused
Yes, because fingerprints may be taken only after a final conviction
No, because the right against self-incrimination applies only to civil cases
r: The privilege protects against being compelled to testify or give communicative evidence; taking fingerprints, photographs or blood samples is not covered.
The right does not extend to the mechanical taking of physical evidence.
Fingerprints may be taken during booking, long before conviction.
The right applies to criminal cases and to proceedings where the answer may incriminate.
e: The right against self-incrimination is limited to testimonial compulsion; it is not violated by examining the body of the accused.

q: A family learns that soldiers took their relative and the authorities deny holding him. Which remedy specifically addresses this threat to his life, liberty and security?
a: Writ of amparo
Writ of habeas data
Writ of kalikasan
Petition for certiorari
r: The writ of amparo is the remedy for violations or threats to the right to life, liberty and security, including enforced disappearances.
Habeas data protects the right to privacy regarding data gathered about a person.
The writ of kalikasan is for environmental damage affecting two or more cities or provinces.
Certiorari corrects grave abuse of discretion by a tribunal; it is not a protection writ for disappearances.
e: Amparo covers extralegal killings and enforced disappearances; habeas corpus covers illegal detention; habeas data covers unlawful data gathering.
l: Rule on the Writ of Amparo, A.M. No. 07-9-12-SC

q: Which characteristic of criminal law means that it binds all persons who live or sojourn in the Philippines?
a: Generality
Territoriality
Prospectivity
Legality
r: Generality means penal laws are obligatory on all who live or sojourn in Philippine territory, subject to treaties and international law.
Territoriality means penal laws apply to acts committed within Philippine territory.
Prospectivity means penal laws act on the future and not on past acts, unless favorable to the accused.
Legality (nullum crimen sine lege) means no act is a crime unless a law punishes it.
e: The three main characteristics of criminal law are generality, territoriality and prospectivity.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 2; Civil Code, Art. 14

q: Under the Revised Penal Code, felonies committed by means of fault are called what?
a: Culpable felonies
Intentional felonies
Complex crimes
Continuing crimes
r: Felonies committed by fault (culpa) result from imprudence, negligence, lack of foresight or lack of skill.
Intentional felonies are committed by means of deceit (dolo).
A complex crime is a single act producing two or more felonies, or an offense that is a necessary means to commit another.
A continuing crime is a series of acts arising from one criminal impulse.
e: Article 3 classifies felonies into those committed by deceit (dolo) and those committed by fault (culpa).

q: What do you call a single act that results in two or more grave or less grave felonies?
a: Compound crime
Composite crime
Continued crime
Impossible crime
r: Under Article 48, when a single act constitutes two or more grave or less grave felonies, it is a compound crime.
A composite or special complex crime is one the law treats as a single crime, such as robbery with homicide.
A continued crime is a series of acts from a single criminal impulse.
An impossible crime is an act that would be a crime against persons or property but for its inherent impossibility.
e: Article 48 covers compound crimes (one act, several felonies) and complex crimes proper (one offense as a necessary means to commit another).

q: A persuaded B with a promise of money to kill C, and B killed C. How are A and B liable?
a: Both are principals: A by induction and B by direct participation
A is an accomplice and B is the principal by direct participation
A is an accessory and B is the principal by direct participation
Only B is liable because A did not take part in the killing
r: Article 17 makes a principal both the one who directly takes part and the one who directly forces or induces another to commit the crime.
An accomplice cooperates through previous or simultaneous acts, but A's inducement was the determining cause of the crime.
Accessories act only after the crime, such as concealing it; A acted before.
Inducement for a price makes A a principal even if he did not take part in the act itself.
e: There are three kinds of principals: by direct participation, by induction, and by indispensable cooperation.

q: After a murder, D, who had no part in the crime, buried the victim's body to keep the police from finding it. What is D's liability?
a: Accessory, for concealing the body to prevent discovery of the crime
Principal by indispensable cooperation in the murder
Accomplice, for cooperating in the execution of the murder
None, because burying a body is not punishable
r: Article 19 makes an accessory one who, after the crime, conceals or destroys the body of the crime to prevent its discovery.
Indispensable cooperation must happen in the execution of the crime, not after it.
An accomplice cooperates by previous or simultaneous acts, not by acts after the crime.
Concealing the body to prevent discovery is a punishable act of an accessory.
e: Accessories take part after the commission of the crime by profiting from it, concealing it, or helping the principal escape.

q: E, the wife of a thief, hid the stolen jewelry to protect her husband from arrest; she did not profit from it. Is she criminally liable as an accessory?
a: No, because a spouse who acts as an accessory without profiting is exempt
Yes, because concealing the effects of a crime is always punishable
Yes, but only as an accomplice because she is his wife
No, because concealment of stolen things is not an act of an accessory
r: Article 20 exempts the spouse, ascendants, descendants, siblings and relatives by affinity in the same degrees, except those who profit from the crime.
The law exempts certain relatives precisely because of their relationship, unless they profited.
Her act came after the crime, so she could only be an accessory, and the exemption applies.
Concealing the effects of a crime is an act of an accessory under Article 19, but she is exempt under Article 20.
e: The exemption of relatives in Article 20 does not cover accessories who profit or help the offender profit from the crime.

q: F and G agreed to rob a store and planned how to do it, but they were arrested before they took any further step. Robbery is not among the felonies where conspiracy is specially punished. What is their liability?
a: None yet, because mere conspiracy to rob is not punishable by law
Attempted robbery, because they had already agreed on the plan
Frustrated robbery, because only their arrest stopped them
Consummated robbery, because conspiracy makes the act of one the act of all
r: Article 8 punishes conspiracy and proposal only in cases specially provided by law, such as treason, rebellion and sedition, so a bare agreement to rob is not a crime.
An attempt requires overt acts that directly begin the commission of the felony; agreeing and planning are only preparatory.
A frustrated stage requires all acts of execution to be performed.
Conspiracy as a manner of committing a crime makes the act of one the act of all only once the crime is executed.
e: Conspiracy may be a crime in itself (only where the law punishes it) or a manner of incurring liability once the planned crime is carried out.

q: H stabbed I in the chest with intent to kill, inflicting a mortal wound, but a doctor saved I's life through timely surgery. What stage of the felony was committed?
a: Frustrated homicide
Attempted homicide
Consummated homicide
Physical injuries only
r: The offender performed all the acts of execution that would produce death, but death did not follow because of a cause independent of his will, the medical help.
An attempt means the offender did not perform all the acts of execution; here he did.
The felony is consummated only if the victim dies.
Intent to kill and a mortal wound make this a homicide case, not mere physical injuries.
e: In crimes against persons, a mortal wound with intent to kill, followed by survival due to medical aid, is typically the frustrated stage.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the attempted from the frustrated stage of a felony?
a: In the attempted stage not all acts of execution are performed; in the frustrated stage all are, but the felony is not produced
In the attempted stage the felony is produced; in the frustrated stage it is not
The attempted stage needs intent to kill; the frustrated stage does not
The attempted stage applies only to crimes against property; the frustrated stage only to crimes against persons
r: Article 6 defines the attempted stage by incomplete acts of execution and the frustrated stage by complete acts that fail to produce the felony for causes independent of the offender's will.
In both stages the felony is not produced.
Intent is required in both stages; the difference lies in the acts of execution.
Both stages can apply to different kinds of felonies, although some crimes, like theft, have no frustrated stage.
e: The key difference is whether the offender has performed all the acts of execution.

q: A felony is punishable by arresto menor or a fine not exceeding forty thousand pesos. How is it classified according to gravity?
a: Light felony
Less grave felony
Grave felony
Afflictive felony
r: Article 9, as amended by R.A. 10951, defines light felonies as those punishable by arresto menor or a fine not exceeding P40,000, or both.
Less grave felonies are punished with correctional penalties.
Grave felonies are punished with capital or afflictive penalties.
Afflictive is a class of penalty, not a separate class of felony under Article 9.
e: Felonies are grave, less grave or light depending on the penalty attached to them.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 9, as amended by R.A. 10951

q: J was suddenly attacked with a knife by K. J grabbed a piece of wood and hit K once, disabling him. J did not provoke the attack. Which circumstance applies to J?
a: Self-defense, a justifying circumstance
Passion or obfuscation, a mitigating circumstance
Accident, an exempting circumstance
Uncontrollable fear, an exempting circumstance
r: There was unlawful aggression by K, reasonable necessity of the means J used, and lack of sufficient provocation on J's part, the three requisites of self-defense.
J acted to repel an attack, not out of a passion that merely reduces liability.
Accident requires a lawful act done with due care that causes injury by mere accident; J acted deliberately to defend himself.
J's act was a defense against an actual attack, not compulsion by fear of a threatened injury.
e: Justifying circumstances make the act lawful, so the person incurs neither criminal nor civil liability.

q: L, who suffers from a mental illness that totally deprived him of reason at the time, killed his neighbor. Which circumstance applies?
a: Insanity, an exempting circumstance
Self-defense, a justifying circumstance
Lack of intent, a mitigating circumstance
Lucid interval, an aggravating circumstance
r: An insane person who acts without a lucid interval is exempt from criminal liability, although civil liability may remain.
There was no unlawful aggression from the neighbor to justify the act.
Insanity that totally deprives a person of reason exempts him entirely, not merely mitigates.
If L had acted during a lucid interval, he would be liable, but a lucid interval is not an aggravating circumstance.
e: Exempting circumstances recognize that the act is wrongful but the actor lacks intelligence, freedom or intent.

q: After committing homicide, M went to the police station on his own and surrendered before any warrant was issued. How does this affect his liability?
a: It is a mitigating circumstance of voluntary surrender
It is an exempting circumstance that frees him from liability
It is a justifying circumstance that makes the killing lawful
It has no effect because he already committed the crime
r: Article 13(7) treats voluntary surrender to a person in authority or his agents as mitigating when it is spontaneous and the offender is not yet under arrest.
Surrender after the crime cannot remove liability; it only lowers the penalty.
Nothing in his surrender makes the killing lawful.
The law rewards spontaneous surrender by mitigating the penalty.
e: Voluntary surrender is mitigating when the offender has not been arrested, surrenders to a person in authority or an agent, and does so spontaneously.

q: N attacked a sleeping man who had no chance to defend himself, choosing that means so the victim could not resist. What circumstance attended the killing?
a: Treachery (alevosia)
Evident premeditation
Nighttime
Abuse of superior strength
r: Treachery exists when the offender employs means that directly and specially ensure the execution of the crime without risk to himself from any defense by the victim.
Evident premeditation requires proof of a plan, the lapse of sufficient time, and acts showing the offender clung to his decision.
Nighttime is aggravating only when purposely sought to facilitate the crime.
Abuse of superior strength involves a notorious disparity of force, not the victim's helplessness in sleep.
e: Attacking a sleeping or helpless victim, deliberately chosen to prevent defense, is a classic example of treachery, which qualifies a killing to murder.

q: O, a habitual drunkard, killed a man while intoxicated. How is the intoxication treated?
a: As an aggravating circumstance, because the intoxication is habitual
As a mitigating circumstance, because drunkenness reduces control
As an exempting circumstance, because he was not in his right mind
As a justifying circumstance, because he acted without intent
r: Under Article 15, intoxication is aggravating if it is habitual or intentional (taken to commit the felony).
Intoxication is mitigating only if it is neither habitual nor subsequent to the plan to commit the felony.
Intoxication is an alternative circumstance; it never exempts.
Intoxication cannot make an unlawful act lawful.
e: Relationship, intoxication and degree of education are alternative circumstances that may aggravate or mitigate depending on the facts.

q: A boat was sinking, so P threw cargo owned by Q overboard to keep the boat afloat and save the passengers. What applies to P?
a: State of necessity, a justifying circumstance, though civil liability may arise
Accident, an exempting circumstance with no civil liability
Lawful exercise of a right, an exempting circumstance
Obedience to an order, a mitigating circumstance
r: Article 11(4) justifies causing damage to avoid a greater evil that actually exists when there is no less harmful means; the persons benefited may be civilly liable under Article 101.
The damage was deliberate, not accidental.
Fulfillment of duty or lawful exercise of a right is a separate justifying circumstance and does not fit these facts.
No superior gave P an order.
e: State of necessity is the justifying circumstance where civil liability remains, borne by those who benefited.

q: Which of the following totally extinguishes criminal liability?
a: Absolute pardon
Commutation of sentence
Conditional pardon
Parole
r: Article 89 lists absolute pardon among the causes of total extinction of criminal liability.
Commutation only reduces the penalty and is a partial extinction.
Conditional pardon partially extinguishes liability; violating its conditions revives the penalty.
Parole suspends the service of the rest of the sentence; it does not totally extinguish liability.
e: Total extinction (Art. 89) includes death of the convict, service of sentence, amnesty, absolute pardon, prescription of the crime or penalty, and marriage of the offended woman under Art. 344.

q: How does amnesty differ from pardon?
a: Amnesty needs Congress's concurrence and erases the offense; pardon follows conviction
Amnesty is granted only to individuals; pardon is granted to classes of persons
Amnesty is granted by the courts; pardon is granted by Congress
Amnesty restores only civil rights; pardon erases the offense itself
r: Amnesty is a public act, usually for political offenses, granted by the President with the concurrence of a majority of Congress, and it obliterates the offense; pardon is granted by the President after final conviction.
Amnesty is usually granted to classes of persons; pardon is granted to individuals.
Both are executive acts; neither is granted by the courts.
Amnesty, not pardon, looks backward and abolishes the offense.
e: Both are acts of executive clemency under Art. VII, Sec. 19 of the Constitution.
l: 1987 Constitution, Art. VII, Sec. 19; Revised Penal Code, Art. 89

q: R was charged with oral defamation, which prescribes in six months. The complaint was filed eight months after the offended party learned of the remarks. What is the effect?
a: Criminal liability is extinguished by prescription of the crime
The accused may still be convicted because the crime is light
The penalty is only reduced because of the delay
The case must first be referred to the Lupon to stop prescription
r: Under Article 90, oral defamation prescribes in six months, so filing after eight months means the crime has prescribed.
Prescription extinguishes liability whatever the classification of the offense.
Prescription bars the prosecution entirely; it does not merely lower the penalty.
Barangay conciliation can suspend prescription only while it is pending; it does not revive a crime that has already prescribed.
e: Article 90 sets periods: 20 years for crimes punished with reclusion perpetua or temporal, 15 years for other afflictive penalties, 10 for correctional penalties (5 for arresto mayor), 1 year for libel, 6 months for oral defamation and slander by deed, and 2 months for light offenses.

q: S died while his appeal from a conviction for estafa was pending. What happens to his criminal liability and to the civil liability based solely on the crime?
a: Both are extinguished, because he died before final judgment
Only the criminal liability is extinguished; his heirs must pay the civil liability arising from the crime
Neither is extinguished, because he was already convicted by the trial court
Only the civil liability is extinguished; the conviction stands
r: Death before final judgment extinguishes criminal liability and the civil liability based solely on the offense (Art. 89(1)).
Civil liability arising solely from the crime dies with the accused if he dies before final judgment; other sources of civil liability may be pursued separately.
A conviction on appeal is not yet final.
The criminal liability is the one first extinguished by death.
e: Death of the convict extinguishes personal penalties and, if before final judgment, pecuniary penalties and civil liability ex delicto.

q: T killed his legitimate father. What crime did he commit?
a: Parricide
Murder
Homicide
Infanticide
r: Article 246 punishes the killing of one's father, mother, child, legitimate ascendant or descendant, or spouse as parricide.
Murder requires a qualifying circumstance and no relationship covered by parricide.
Homicide applies when there is no relationship and no qualifying circumstance.
Infanticide is the killing of a child less than three days old.
e: Relationship is the key element of parricide; it must be alleged and proved.

q: U poisoned his co-worker's coffee to kill him, and the co-worker died. There is no relationship between them. What crime was committed?
a: Murder, qualified by the use of poison
Homicide, because poison is not a qualifying circumstance
Parricide, because they worked together
Physical injuries resulting in death
r: Article 248 qualifies a killing as murder when committed by means of poison, among other circumstances.
Poison is expressly listed as a qualifying circumstance of murder.
Parricide requires a blood or marital relationship covered by Article 246.
Intent to kill and death of the victim make this a killing, not mere physical injuries.
e: Murder is homicide attended by any qualifying circumstance in Article 248, such as treachery, price or reward, poison, fire, evident premeditation or cruelty.

q: A mother killed her two-day-old baby. What crime did she commit?
a: Infanticide
Parricide
Murder
Abortion
r: Article 255 punishes the killing of a child less than three days of age as infanticide.
Parricide covers killing one's child, but when the child is less than three days old the law calls it infanticide.
The age of the child makes it infanticide rather than murder.
Abortion involves the killing of a fetus before birth; the child here was already born.
e: If the mother kills the child to conceal her dishonor, the penalty is lower, but the crime is still infanticide.

q: V fired a gun at W during an argument without intent to kill. W was not hit. What crime was committed?
a: Illegal discharge of firearm
Attempted homicide with a firearm
Grave threats
Alarm and scandal
r: Article 254 punishes discharging a firearm against or at another person when there is no intent to kill.
Attempted homicide requires intent to kill.
Grave threats involve threatening another with a wrong amounting to a crime, not actually firing at him.
Alarm and scandal covers firing a gun in a public place to cause alarm, not firing at a specific person.
e: The presence or absence of intent to kill separates illegal discharge of firearm from attempted or frustrated homicide.

q: X punched Y, intending only to hurt him, but Y fell, hit his head and died. What is X's liability?
a: Homicide, mitigated by lack of intent to commit so grave a wrong
Physical injuries only, because he had no intent to kill
Murder, because the victim died from the attack
No liability, because the death was accidental
r: One who commits a felony is liable for all its direct consequences (Art. 4), but the lack of intent to cause so grave a wrong is mitigating (Art. 13(3)).
Liability follows the result when death is the direct, natural and logical consequence of the felonious act.
There is no qualifying circumstance to make it murder.
The punch was a felonious act, so the death is not an accident under Article 12(4).
e: Article 4 makes the offender liable for the result of his felony, even if different from what he intended (praeter intentionem).

q: Which element separates rape by sexual assault from rape by sexual intercourse under Article 266-A?
a: The act, such as inserting an object or instrument into the genital or anal orifice
The use of force, which is required only in rape by sexual assault
The age of the victim, which must be below 16 in rape by sexual assault
The sex of the offender, who must be a woman in rape by sexual assault
r: Rape by sexual assault is committed by inserting the penis into another's mouth or anal orifice, or any instrument or object into the genital or anal orifice.
Force, threat or intimidation may be present in both kinds of rape.
Age below 16 relates to statutory rape, not to the distinction between the two modes.
Either kind of rape may be committed by any person under the law; the act is what differs.
e: R.A. 8353 reclassified rape as a crime against persons and created rape by sexual assault; R.A. 11648 raised the age for statutory rape to below 16.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 266-A, as amended by R.A. 8353 and R.A. 11648

q: A victim of a mauling was unable to work for 35 days. Which classification of physical injuries applies?
a: Serious physical injuries
Less serious physical injuries
Slight physical injuries
Mutilation
r: Article 263 makes injuries serious when they incapacitate the victim for labor for more than 30 days.
Less serious physical injuries cover incapacity or medical attendance of 10 days or more but not more than 30 days.
Slight physical injuries cover 1 to 9 days of incapacity or medical attendance.
Mutilation requires deliberate cutting off of a body part.
e: The period of incapacity or medical attendance is the usual basis for classifying physical injuries.

q: Z shot two persons in separate bursts during one quarrel, killing both, without any qualifying circumstance. How many crimes did he commit?
a: Two separate homicides, because there were separate acts
One compound crime of double homicide
One complex crime, because the killings were related
One homicide, because the quarrel was a single event
r: Separate acts of shooting, each producing a death, give rise to separate felonies.
A compound crime requires a single act producing two or more grave or less grave felonies.
A complex crime proper requires one offense to be a necessary means of committing another.
Each killing by a separate act is a separate homicide, even within one event.
e: Whether the deaths came from a single act or from several acts decides between a compound crime and separate crimes.

q: What element distinguishes robbery from theft?
a: Violence against or intimidation of persons, or force upon things
Intent to gain on the part of the offender
Taking of personal property belonging to another
Absence of the owner's consent
r: Robbery is the taking of personal property with violence or intimidation of persons or force upon things; theft is committed without these.
Intent to gain is an element of both theft and robbery.
Taking personal property of another is common to both.
Lack of consent is common to both.
e: Theft (Art. 308) and robbery (Art. 293) share most elements; the means of taking separates them.

q: What is the essential element of estafa?
a: Damage caused through deceit or abuse of confidence
Taking of property by force upon things
Destruction of property out of hate or revenge
Detention of a person to extract money
r: Estafa under Article 315 requires deceit or abuse of confidence and damage or prejudice capable of pecuniary estimation.
Taking by force upon things is robbery.
Deliberately damaging property is malicious mischief.
Detaining a person for ransom is kidnapping.
e: In estafa the victim parts with the property because of the offender's deceit or abuse of confidence.

q: Five armed men formed a band to commit robberies on the highway. What crime is committed by forming such a band?
a: Brigandage
Robbery in band
Illegal assembly
Kidnapping for ransom
r: Article 306 defines brigandage as more than three armed persons forming a band of robbers to commit robbery in the highway, among other purposes; the mere formation is punished.
Robbery in band requires an actual robbery committed by more than three armed persons.
Illegal assembly involves a meeting to commit crimes under the RPC, but forming a band of highway robbers is specifically brigandage.
Kidnapping for ransom requires an actual detention of a person.
e: In brigandage, the purpose of the band is the gravamen; actual robbery need not be committed.

q: A, angry at his neighbor, deliberately destroyed the neighbor's fence. There was no fire, no taking and no intent to gain. What crime was committed?
a: Malicious mischief
Theft
Robbery with force upon things
Arson
r: Article 327 punishes deliberately causing damage to the property of another, not constituting arson or other crimes involving destruction.
There was no taking with intent to gain.
Robbery requires the taking of personal property.
There was no burning, so it is not arson.
e: Malicious mischief requires deliberate damage to another's property, done out of hate, revenge or another evil motive.

q: A private individual kept a minor locked in a room for two days without any legal ground. What crime was committed?
a: Serious illegal detention, because the victim is a minor
Slight illegal detention, because it lasted only two days
Arbitrary detention, because the victim was deprived of liberty
Unlawful arrest, because the victim was detained
r: Under Article 267, detention by a private individual is serious when the victim is a minor, whatever the duration.
The minority of the victim makes the detention serious even if it lasted less than three days.
Arbitrary detention is committed by a public officer, not a private individual.
Unlawful arrest involves detaining a person to deliver him to the authorities without legal ground.
e: Kidnapping and serious illegal detention apply when the detention lasts more than three days, simulates public authority, involves serious injuries or threats to kill, or the victim is a minor, a female or a public officer.

q: B threatened to kill C unless C paid him P20,000, and C paid. What crime did B commit?
a: Grave threats, with the condition attained
Robbery with violence against persons
Light coercion
Estafa through deceit
r: Article 282 punishes threatening another with a wrong amounting to a crime, here death, under a condition such as a demand for money; the penalty is higher when the purpose is attained.
Robbery requires taking with immediate violence or intimidation; threats of future harm with a demand are grave threats.
Coercion involves preventing or compelling an act by violence or threats, but threats to kill with a demand for money are specifically grave threats.
No deceit was used to obtain the money.
e: Grave threats concern a future wrong amounting to a crime; coercion concerns immediate compulsion.

q: A police officer detained a person for several hours without any legal ground. What crime did the officer commit?
a: Arbitrary detention
Serious illegal detention
Unlawful arrest
Grave coercion
r: Article 124 punishes a public officer or employee who detains a person without legal grounds.
Illegal detention is committed by private individuals.
Unlawful arrest under Article 269 is committed by any person who arrests another to deliver him to the authorities without reasonable ground.
Grave coercion involves compelling or preventing an act, not detention without legal ground by a public officer.
e: The offender's status as a public officer is the key element of arbitrary detention.

q: Armed men who were not passengers or crew boarded a fishing boat in Philippine waters and took its catch by force. What crime was committed?
a: Piracy in Philippine waters
Mutiny on the high seas
Robbery in an inhabited place
Brigandage
r: Piracy is committed by persons who are not passengers or members of the crew who attack or seize a vessel or its cargo; P.D. 532 and Article 122 cover Philippine waters.
Mutiny is committed by the crew or passengers against the authority of the master.
Robbery in an inhabited place concerns houses and buildings, not vessels.
Brigandage concerns bands of robbers on land, especially highways.
e: Piracy is committed by outsiders; mutiny by those on board.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 122, as amended by R.A. 7659; P.D. 532

q: A barangay tanod on duty was punched by a resident because the tanod was enforcing a curfew. What crime did the resident commit?
a: Direct assault, because he attacked an agent of a person in authority performing his duty
Slight physical injuries only, because a tanod is a private individual
Grave coercion, because he resisted the curfew
Alarm and scandal, because it happened in public
r: Article 148 punishes attacking or employing force against a person in authority or his agent while engaged in the performance of official duties; a barangay tanod is an agent of a person in authority.
Barangay tanods are agents of persons in authority under the Local Government Code.
The resident did not compel or prevent an act by violence; he attacked an agent on duty.
Alarm and scandal concerns disturbances of public peace, not assaults on authorities.
e: The victim's status and the fact that he was performing his duty make the attack direct assault.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 148; R.A. 7160, Sec. 388

q: A jail guard, through negligence, left a cell unlocked, and a detainee escaped. What crime did the guard commit?
a: Infidelity in the custody of prisoners through negligence
Conniving with or consenting to the escape of a prisoner
Delivering prisoners from jail
Evasion of service of sentence
r: Article 224 punishes a public officer whose negligence allows a prisoner under his custody to escape.
Connivance (Art. 223) requires consent or agreement to the escape, not mere negligence.
Delivering prisoners from jail (Art. 156) is committed by an outsider who helps the escape.
Evasion of service of sentence is committed by the convict who escapes, not by the guard.
e: Infidelity in the custody of prisoners covers connivance (Art. 223) and negligence (Art. 224) by public officers.

q: A traffic enforcer agreed to accept P5,000 in exchange for not issuing a ticket he was supposed to issue. What crime did he commit?
a: Direct bribery
Indirect bribery
Qualified bribery
Corruption of public officials
r: Article 210 punishes a public officer who agrees to refrain from doing something which is his official duty in consideration of a gift or promise.
Indirect bribery is accepting gifts offered by reason of one's office, without an agreement to perform or refrain from an act.
Qualified bribery applies to law enforcers who refrain from arresting or prosecuting offenders of crimes punishable by reclusion perpetua or death.
Corruption of public officials is the crime of the one who offers the bribe.
e: The giver is liable for corruption of public officials (Art. 212); the receiving officer for bribery.

q: In front of guests at a party, D slapped E to humiliate him. What crime did D commit?
a: Slander by deed
Grave oral defamation
Intriguing against honor
Slight physical injuries
r: Article 359 punishes performing an act, not words, that casts dishonor, discredit or contempt upon another.
Oral defamation is committed through spoken words.
Intriguing against honor is a scheme or plot to blemish reputation, usually by spreading rumors.
When the purpose of the slap is to humiliate rather than to injure, it is slander by deed.
e: The intent to humiliate, shown by the circumstances, makes a slap slander by deed.

q: F secretly spread rumors among neighbors that a teacher was having an affair, without saying where the story came from, to ruin the teacher's reputation. What crime did F commit?
a: Intriguing against honor
Slander by deed
Libel by means of writings
Grave scandal
r: Article 364 punishes any intrigue whose principal purpose is to blemish the honor or reputation of another, where the source of the defamatory story is hard to trace.
Slander by deed requires an act, not the spreading of a story.
Libel requires a public and malicious imputation made in writing or similar means.
Grave scandal concerns highly scandalous conduct offensive to decency, not rumors about another.
e: Intriguing against honor typically involves gossip or rumor-mongering whose source cannot be determined.

q: A married man kept his mistress in the conjugal dwelling. What crime did he commit?
a: Concubinage
Adultery
Bigamy
Seduction
r: Article 334 punishes a husband who keeps a mistress in the conjugal dwelling, has sexual intercourse under scandalous circumstances, or cohabits with her elsewhere.
Adultery is committed by a married woman and the man who knows she is married.
Bigamy requires a second marriage while the first is subsisting.
Seduction involves having sexual intercourse with a woman through abuse of confidence or deceit.
e: Concubinage and adultery may be prosecuted only upon complaint of the offended spouse.

q: G, whose first marriage was never annulled or declared void, married H. What crime did G commit?
a: Bigamy
Concubinage
Illegal marriage
Adultery
r: Article 349 punishes contracting a second or subsequent marriage before the first marriage has been legally dissolved or the absent spouse has been declared presumptively dead.
Concubinage concerns a husband's relations with a mistress, not a second marriage.
Bigamy is the specific crime for marrying while a prior marriage subsists.
Adultery concerns sexual relations, not the contracting of marriage.
e: A judicial declaration of nullity of the first marriage must be obtained before remarrying; otherwise bigamy may be committed.

q: Against her will and with lewd designs, a man took a woman away from her home. What crime did he commit?
a: Forcible abduction
Consented abduction
Simple seduction
Slight illegal detention
r: Article 342 punishes taking away a woman against her will and with lewd designs.
Consented abduction requires the woman's consent, given within the age limits set by law.
Seduction involves sexual intercourse obtained through deceit or abuse of authority, not a taking away against her will.
Lewd designs make the act forcible abduction rather than illegal detention.
e: Lewd design is the element that makes the taking an abduction rather than another crime against liberty.

q: A married woman had sexual relations with a man who knew she was married. Who may be held liable for adultery?
a: Both the married woman and the man
Only the married woman
Only the man, as the guilty party
Neither, unless a public prosecutor files the complaint
r: Article 333 punishes both the married woman and the man who has carnal knowledge of her knowing her to be married.
The law punishes both participants.
Both are liable; the woman is the principal offender in adultery.
Adultery cannot be prosecuted except upon complaint of the offended spouse, who must include both guilty parties.
e: Under Article 344, the offended spouse must file the complaint against both guilty parties, if both are alive.

q: Which law is the Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2012?
r: R.A. 10364 amended R.A. 9208 and expanded the acts of trafficking in persons; it was later amended again by R.A. 11862.
R.A. 9208 is the original Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2003.
R.A. 11313 is the Safe Spaces Act.
R.A. 11053 is the Anti-Hazing Act of 2018.
e: Trafficking involves recruitment, transport, harboring or receipt of persons by means such as force, fraud or abuse of power for exploitation.
l: R.A. 9208, as amended by R.A. 10364 and R.A. 11862

q: What law punishes catcalling, wolf-whistling and other gender-based sexual harassment in streets and public places?
a: R.A. 11313, the Safe Spaces Act
R.A. 7877, the Anti-Sexual Harassment Act of 1995
R.A. 9262, the Anti-VAWC Act of 2004
R.A. 11053, the Anti-Hazing Act of 2018
r: R.A. 11313 penalizes gender-based sexual harassment in streets, public spaces, online, workplaces and educational institutions.
R.A. 7877 covers sexual harassment in work, education and training environments involving authority or influence.
R.A. 9262 covers violence against women and their children in intimate relationships.
R.A. 11053 covers hazing in organizations.
e: The Safe Spaces Act is also known as the Bawal Bastos Law.

q: Which law is the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020?
r: R.A. 11479 repealed the Human Security Act and is the current Anti-Terrorism Act.
R.A. 9372, the Human Security Act of 2007, was repealed by R.A. 11479.
R.A. 10168 is the Terrorism Financing Prevention and Suppression Act of 2012.
R.A. 10175 is the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012.
e: R.A. 11479 defines terrorism by its acts and its purposes, such as intimidating the public or seriously destabilizing the country.

q: Under the Anti-Hazing Act of 2018, what is hazing?
a: Any act causing physical or psychological harm to a recruit as a condition of admission
Any initiation rite held by a fraternity without a faculty adviser
Any act of bullying committed against a classmate in school
Any public ridicule of a member of a sorority or fraternity
r: R.A. 11053 defines hazing as any physical or psychological suffering, harm or injury inflicted on a recruit, neophyte or applicant as a requirement for admission or continued membership.
The presence or absence of a faculty adviser does not define hazing.
Bullying among students is covered by the Anti-Bullying Act of 2013.
Hazing is defined by its connection to admission or membership, not by mere ridicule.
e: R.A. 11053 prohibits all forms of hazing and regulates initiation rites that involve no physical or psychological harm.

q: Under the anti-trafficking law, when is the recruitment of a child for exploitation considered trafficking even without force, fraud or coercion?
a: Always; the means need not be proved when the victim is a child
Only when the child is below 12 years old
Only when the child is taken outside the country
Only when the parents of the child did not consent
r: R.A. 9208 as amended treats the recruitment, transport or harboring of a child for exploitation as trafficking even if none of the means is used.
The law protects all persons below 18 years of age, not only those below 12.
Trafficking may be domestic or across borders.
Consent of the child or the parents is not a defense in child trafficking.
e: A child is a person below 18, or over 18 but unable to fully protect himself because of a disability.
l: R.A. 9208, Secs. 3-4, as amended by R.A. 10364

q: What quantum of evidence is required to convict an accused in a criminal case?
a: Proof beyond reasonable doubt
Preponderance of evidence
Substantial evidence
Clear and convincing evidence
r: Rule 133, Section 2 requires proof beyond reasonable doubt, or moral certainty, for conviction.
Preponderance of evidence is the standard in civil cases.
Substantial evidence is the standard in administrative and quasi-judicial cases.
Clear and convincing evidence is used in certain special matters, not for criminal conviction.
e: Proof beyond reasonable doubt does not mean absolute certainty; it means moral certainty that convinces an unprejudiced mind.

q: What is the equipoise rule?
a: When the evidence of both sides is evenly balanced, the party with the burden of proof loses
When the evidence is evenly balanced, the court must order a new trial
When both parties present the same number of witnesses, the case is dismissed
When the evidence is balanced, the side with the older documents prevails
r: Under the equipoise (equiponderance) rule, evenly balanced evidence means the party with the burden fails; in criminal cases the accused is acquitted.
Balanced evidence leads to judgment against the party with the burden, not to a new trial.
Evidence is weighed, not counted by the number of witnesses.
The age of documents does not decide balanced evidence.
e: The rule follows from the presumption of innocence and the burden of proof resting on the prosecution.

q: A knife recovered from the crime scene is shown to the court so the judge can see it. What form of evidence is it?
a: Object evidence
Documentary evidence
Testimonial evidence
Hearsay evidence
r: Object (real) evidence is addressed to the senses of the court and may be exhibited, examined or viewed.
Documentary evidence consists of writings or materials offered for their contents.
Testimonial evidence is given by a witness under oath.
Hearsay concerns out-of-court statements offered for their truth.
e: The three forms of evidence are object, documentary and testimonial.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 130, Sec. 1 (2019 Revised Rules on Evidence)

q: A letter is presented to prove what is written in it. What form of evidence is it?
a: Documentary evidence
Object evidence
Testimonial evidence
Circumstantial evidence
r: Documents are writings, recordings, photographs or other materials offered as proof of their contents.
If the letter were offered to prove its existence or physical condition rather than its contents, it would be object evidence.
Testimonial evidence comes from a witness testifying in court.
Circumstantial evidence is a kind of evidence by its relation to the fact, not a form.
e: The purpose of the offer decides whether a writing is documentary or object evidence.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 130, Sec. 2 (2019 Revised Rules on Evidence)

q: A witness testifies that he saw the accused running from the house with a bloody knife moments after a scream, but he did not see the stabbing. What kind of evidence is his testimony as to the killing?
a: Circumstantial evidence
Direct evidence
Negative evidence
Cumulative evidence
r: The testimony proves facts from which the main fact, the killing, may be inferred, so it is circumstantial.
Direct evidence proves the fact in issue without inference, such as an eyewitness to the stabbing.
Negative evidence is testimony that a fact did not happen or was not observed.
Cumulative evidence repeats the same kind of evidence on the same point.
e: Circumstantial evidence may support a conviction if the requisites of Rule 133, Sec. 4 are met.

q: Two witnesses describe the same robbery in the same way, and a third witness adds a detail that supports their account from a different angle. What is the third witness's testimony?
a: Corroborative evidence
Cumulative evidence
Primary evidence
Rebuttal evidence
r: Corroborative evidence is additional evidence of a different kind or source tending to prove the same point.
Cumulative evidence is additional evidence of the same kind and character on the same point.
Primary evidence refers to the original document under the original document rule.
Rebuttal evidence answers new matters raised by the adverse party.
e: Corroborative and cumulative evidence are both additional evidence; they differ in whether the new evidence is of a different kind.

q: When is evidence admissible?
a: When it is relevant and not excluded by the Constitution, the law or the Rules
When it is offered by the prosecution in a criminal case against the accused
When it is notarized or certified by a public officer
When both parties agree that it is true
r: Rule 128, Section 3 makes evidence admissible when it is relevant and competent, meaning not excluded by law or the Rules.
Evidence from either party must meet the same tests of relevance and competence.
Notarization affects how a document is authenticated, not the general test of admissibility.
Admissibility is decided by the court under the Rules, not by agreement of the parties.
e: Admissibility (relevance and competence) is different from weight (credibility and persuasiveness).

q: Which statement best describes the original document rule?
a: When the contents of a document are in issue, the original must be presented, subject to exceptions
Every document must be presented in its original form even if only its existence is in issue
Copies are always admissible as long as they are certified by a lawyer
Oral testimony is preferred over the document when the contents are disputed
r: Rule 130, Section 3 requires the original document when the subject of inquiry is its contents, with listed exceptions such as loss or destruction without bad faith.
The rule applies only when the contents of the document are the subject of inquiry.
Certification by a lawyer does not satisfy the rule.
Oral testimony is not a substitute for the original when the contents are in issue, unless an exception applies.
e: The 2019 Revised Rules on Evidence renamed the best evidence rule as the original document rule.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 130, Sec. 3 (2019 Revised Rules on Evidence)

q: A witness testifies, 'My neighbor told me that the accused stole the cellphone.' The prosecution offers this to prove the theft. How should the court treat it?
a: As hearsay, inadmissible to prove the theft unless an exception applies
As direct evidence, because the witness heard it personally
As admissible, because the neighbor is a trustworthy person
As an admission, because it concerns the accused
r: A statement made out of court, offered to prove the truth of what it asserts, is hearsay and generally inadmissible.
The witness personally heard only the statement, not the theft itself.
Trustworthiness of the declarant does not cure the hearsay problem.
An admission must be the statement of the party himself, not of a neighbor.
e: A witness may testify only to facts within personal knowledge, unless an exception to the hearsay rule applies.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 130 (hearsay rule, 2019 Revised Rules on Evidence)

q: Shortly before dying of stab wounds and knowing he was about to die, the victim named his attacker to a police officer. Is the statement admissible?
a: Yes, as a dying declaration, an exception to the hearsay rule
No, because the victim cannot be cross-examined
No, because it was made to a police officer and not to a judge
Yes, but only as proof of the time of death
r: A statement about the cause and circumstances of death, made under the consciousness of impending death, is admissible as a dying declaration.
The lack of cross-examination is precisely why the law requires consciousness of impending death as a guarantee of truth.
A dying declaration may be made to anyone, not only to a judge.
It is admissible to prove the identity of the attacker and the circumstances of death.
e: The requisites are: it concerns the cause and circumstances of death, made under consciousness of impending death, the declarant was competent, and it is offered in a case involving his death.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 130 (dying declaration, 2019 Revised Rules on Evidence)

q: Why is an extrajudicial confession obtained without the assistance of counsel inadmissible even if it is true?
a: Because the Constitution excludes confessions taken in violation of custodial rights
Because written confessions are always hearsay and cannot be admitted at all
Because a confession must always be made in open court
Because the accused may change his mind before trial
r: Art. III, Sec. 12(3) makes any confession or admission obtained in violation of custodial rights inadmissible, whatever its truth.
A confession of the accused is an admission, which is an exception to the hearsay rule.
Extrajudicial confessions may be admissible if made with the required safeguards.
A valid confession remains admissible even if the accused later recants.
e: Competence of evidence includes constitutional exclusions, which apply even to truthful evidence.

q: Which distinction between the admissibility and the weight of evidence is correct?
a: Admissibility concerns whether evidence may be considered; weight concerns how much it proves
Admissibility is decided by the prosecutor; weight is decided by the judge
Admissibility depends on the number of witnesses; weight depends on their credibility
Admissibility and weight mean the same thing under the Rules
r: Admissibility is about relevance and competence; weight is about the persuasiveness or credibility of evidence already admitted.
Both admissibility and weight are decided by the court.
Neither test depends on the number of witnesses.
They are distinct concepts; admitted evidence may still carry little weight.
e: Evidence may be admitted yet be given little or no weight after the court evaluates it.

q: Under the 2019 Revised Rules on Evidence, when is the testimony of a witness formally offered?
a: At the time the witness is called to testify
After all the documentary exhibits have been marked
Only in the memorandum filed after trial
At the pre-trial conference before any witness testifies
r: Rule 132, Section 35 requires the offer of testimonial evidence at the time the witness is called to testify, stating its purpose.
Documentary and object evidence are offered after the presentation of a party's testimonial evidence.
Evidence must be offered during trial, not only in a memorandum.
Pre-trial is for marking and stipulations, not for the formal offer of testimony.
e: The court considers no evidence that has not been formally offered, and the purpose of the offer must be specified.

q: During direct examination, the prosecutor asks a question that is clearly leading. When should defense counsel object?
a: As soon as the ground for objection becomes reasonably apparent
Only after the witness has finished the entire testimony
Only during the formal offer of documentary evidence
Within five days after receiving the transcript
r: Rule 132, Section 36 requires an objection to a question propounded during oral examination to be made as soon as its grounds become reasonably apparent.
Waiting until the end may result in waiver of the objection.
The formal offer of documents is a separate stage.
Objections to questions must be made during the examination, not days later.
e: Failure to object at the proper time generally waives the objection.

q: Before a private document is received in evidence as authentic, what must be proved?
a: Its due execution and authenticity
Its notarization by a lawyer
Its acceptance by the adverse party
Its registration with a government office
r: Rule 132, Section 20 requires proof of due execution and authenticity of a private document, for example by a witness who saw it executed or by evidence of the genuineness of the signature.
Notarized documents become public documents; private documents need proof of authenticity instead.
The adverse party's acceptance is not required, although an admission may dispense with proof.
Registration is not a general requirement for private documents.
e: Public documents are generally admissible without further proof of due execution; private documents must be authenticated.

q: A party wants to present a photocopy of a contract to prove its terms, claiming the original was destroyed in a fire. What must the party first show?
a: That the original was destroyed without bad faith on the offeror's part
That the photocopy was certified by the barangay captain
That the adverse party has seen the photocopy before
That the contract was signed in the presence of the judge
r: Under the original document rule, secondary evidence of the contents is allowed once the loss or destruction of the original, without bad faith, is shown.
Certification by a barangay captain does not satisfy the rule.
Prior knowledge of the adverse party is not the test.
Signing in the presence of a judge is not required for contracts.
e: Secondary evidence may be a copy, a recital of its contents in an authentic document, or testimony, in that order.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 130, Secs. 3 and 5

q: When is circumstantial evidence sufficient to convict?
a: When there are several proven circumstances that together produce conviction beyond reasonable doubt
When at least one strong circumstance points to the accused
When the accused fails to testify in his own defense
When the circumstances are supported by the sworn testimony of the arresting police officers
r: Rule 133, Section 4 lists these three requisites for conviction on circumstantial evidence.
A single circumstance is not enough under the Rules.
The silence of the accused cannot be used against him.
The source of the evidence does not replace the three requisites.
e: The circumstances must form an unbroken chain leading to one fair and reasonable conclusion pointing to the accused.

q: Is an extrajudicial confession alone sufficient to convict the accused?
a: No, it must be corroborated by evidence of the corpus delicti
Yes, if it was given voluntarily
Yes, if it was written in the accused's own handwriting
No, it can never be used as evidence
r: Rule 133, Section 3 provides that an extrajudicial confession is not sufficient ground for conviction unless corroborated by evidence of the corpus delicti.
Voluntariness makes it admissible but does not make it sufficient alone.
Handwriting does not replace proof of corpus delicti.
A valid extrajudicial confession is admissible; it simply needs corroboration.
e: Corpus delicti means that the crime was actually committed, for example the fact of death in a homicide.

q: A city mayor with salary grade 27 is charged with a graft offense related to his office. Which court has jurisdiction?
a: Sandiganbayan
Regional Trial Court
Court of Appeals
Municipal Trial Court in Cities
r: The Sandiganbayan has jurisdiction over graft and office-related offenses of officials with salary grade 27 or higher, including city mayors.
Office-related cases of officials below salary grade 27 go to the regular trial courts.
The Court of Appeals is an appellate court.
First-level courts do not try graft cases of high-ranking officials.
e: P.D. 1606 as amended by R.A. 10660 defines the jurisdiction of the Sandiganbayan.

q: A crime punishable by imprisonment of eight years was committed in Cebu City. Where must the case be filed?
a: Regional Trial Court in Cebu City
Municipal Trial Court in Cities of Cebu City
Regional Trial Court in Manila
Any court chosen by the offended party
r: Offenses punishable by more than six years fall within the RTC, and venue in criminal cases is where the offense was committed.
First-level courts try offenses punishable by not more than six years.
Venue lies where the crime was committed, not in Manila.
The offended party cannot choose the venue; it is fixed by law.
e: In criminal cases venue is jurisdictional: the case must be filed where the offense or any of its essential elements occurred.
l: B.P. 129, as amended; Rules of Court, Rule 110, Sec. 15

q: Why is venue considered jurisdictional in criminal cases but not in civil cases?
a: Because a criminal court can try only offenses committed within its territory
Because criminal cases are always filed in the Supreme Court
Because the accused chooses the venue in criminal cases
Because civil cases are not governed by the Rules of Court
r: The territorial jurisdiction of a criminal court is limited to offenses committed within it, so improper venue means lack of jurisdiction.
Criminal cases are filed in trial courts, not in the Supreme Court.
Venue is fixed by law, not chosen by the accused.
Civil cases are governed by the Rules of Court; there, venue is procedural and may be waived.
e: Territorial jurisdiction in criminal cases cannot be waived by the parties.

q: How does the court acquire jurisdiction over the person of the accused?
a: By his arrest or his voluntary surrender to the court
By the filing of the complaint with the prosecutor
By the issuance of a subpoena to the accused
By the publication of the information in a newspaper
r: Jurisdiction over the person of the accused is acquired through arrest or voluntary appearance or surrender.
Filing with the prosecutor starts the preliminary investigation, not the court's jurisdiction over the accused.
A subpoena is not the means by which the court acquires jurisdiction over an accused.
Publication is not a mode of acquiring jurisdiction over the accused in criminal cases.
e: Jurisdiction over the subject matter is conferred by law; over the person, by arrest or voluntary surrender.

q: What is the difference between a complaint and an information?
a: A complaint is signed by the offended party or a peace officer; an information is signed by the prosecutor
A complaint is filed only in the RTC; an information only in the MTC
A complaint is oral; an information is written
A complaint charges a crime; an information charges only a violation of an ordinance
r: Rule 110 defines a complaint as a sworn statement subscribed by the offended party, a peace officer or another enforcement officer, and an information as an accusation subscribed by the prosecutor.
Both may be filed in any court with jurisdiction.
Both must be in writing.
Both may charge any offense within the court's jurisdiction.
e: Every criminal action is commenced by a complaint or an information.

q: The accused chose not to testify during trial. The judge remarked that his silence showed guilt. Was the judge correct?
a: No, because the accused may choose not to testify and his silence cannot prejudice him
Yes, because an innocent person would always take the witness stand to deny the charge
Yes, because silence during trial is an implied admission of guilt by the accused
No, unless the prosecution objected to his silence
r: Rule 115 and Art. III, Sec. 17 give the accused the right to testify or not, and his refusal shall not prejudice him.
The law does not presume guilt from silence.
Silence during trial is not an implied admission.
The right does not depend on any objection by the prosecution.
e: The rights of the accused at trial include presumption of innocence, the right to be heard, the right to confront witnesses, and the right against self-incrimination.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 115; 1987 Constitution, Art. III, Secs. 14 and 17

q: The prosecution wants to use the sworn statement of a witness who will not appear at trial, so the defense cannot cross-examine him. Which right of the accused is affected?
a: The right to confront and cross-examine witnesses
The right to a speedy disposition of the case
The right to bail
The right to appeal
r: The accused has the right to meet the witnesses face to face and to cross-examine them; affidavits of absent witnesses are generally inadmissible against him.
Speedy disposition concerns delay, not the use of absent witnesses' statements.
Bail concerns provisional liberty.
Appeal concerns review after judgment.
e: Confrontation allows the accused to test the credibility of the witnesses against him.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 115, Sec. 1(f); 1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 14(2)

q: An accused was charged with homicide, but the information did not allege any qualifying circumstance. After trial, the evidence showed treachery. Can he be convicted of murder?
a: No, because he has the right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation
Yes, because the evidence presented at trial proved the qualifying circumstance
Yes, if the judge believes the evidence is strong
No, because treachery can never be proved by evidence
r: Qualifying and aggravating circumstances must be alleged in the information; otherwise the accused cannot be convicted of the graver offense.
Proof of an unalleged qualifying circumstance does not justify conviction for the graver crime.
The judge's belief cannot override the requirement of allegation.
Treachery may be proved, but it must first be alleged.
e: Rule 110, Sections 8 and 9 require that qualifying and aggravating circumstances be stated in the information.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 110, Secs. 8-9; 1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 14(2)

q: Police officers saw a man stab another person on the street and arrested him on the spot without a warrant. Was the arrest valid?
a: Yes, because it was an in flagrante delicto arrest
No, because a warrant is always needed to arrest a person
Yes, but only if the victim filed a complaint first
No, because only the barangay captain may arrest without a warrant
r: Rule 113, Section 5(a) allows a warrantless arrest when the person has committed, is committing or is attempting an offense in the presence of the arresting officer.
Warrantless arrests are allowed in the cases listed in Rule 113, Section 5.
No prior complaint is needed for an in flagrante arrest.
Any peace officer or private person may arrest in these cases.
e: The three valid warrantless arrests are in flagrante delicto, hot pursuit, and arrest of escaped prisoners.

q: Officers arrived two days after a robbery and arrested a suspect without a warrant, based only on a description from witnesses. Why was this arrest likely invalid?
a: The offense had not 'just been committed' and the officers lacked personal knowledge
Robbery is not one of the offenses for which a warrantless arrest is ever allowed
The witnesses had no right to describe the suspect
Warrantless arrests are allowed only at night
r: A hot pursuit arrest under Rule 113, Section 5(b) requires that the offense has just been committed and that the officers have probable cause based on personal knowledge of facts or circumstances.
Robbery is an offense for which a person may be arrested.
Witness descriptions may support a warrant application but do not by themselves justify a warrantless arrest days later.
There is no rule limiting warrantless arrests to nighttime.
e: Immediacy and personal knowledge of the arresting officer are the requirements for hot pursuit arrests.

q: Officers have a search warrant for a house to look for unlicensed firearms. Which action best complies with the Rules?
a: Search in the presence of the occupant or two witnesses of the locality, and issue a receipt for items seized
Search the house next door as well, since the firearms might have been moved there
Keep the warrant for a month and search the house whenever convenient
Search at night without notice to avoid tipping off the occupants
r: Rule 126 requires the search in the presence of the lawful occupant or a member of the family, or two witnesses of sufficient age residing in the same locality, and a detailed receipt for property seized.
The warrant authorizes a search only of the place particularly described.
A search warrant is valid for only ten days from its date.
A search warrant is served in the day unless the warrant itself allows service at any time.
e: Strict compliance with Rule 126 protects the admissibility of the evidence seized.

q: At a checkpoint, an officer notices a firearm in plain view on the seat of a car. What is the most appropriate legal assessment?
a: The firearm may be seized because it is in plain view during a lawful checkpoint inspection
The firearm may not be seized because the officer has no search warrant
The car may be searched thoroughly because all checkpoint searches are lawful
The officer must first ask the barangay to issue a seizure order
r: The plain view doctrine allows seizure when the officer is lawfully in position, the discovery is inadvertent, and the illegality of the item is immediately apparent.
A warrant is not required for objects in plain view during a lawful intrusion.
Routine checkpoints allow only a visual inspection; a full search needs probable cause.
Barangay officials do not issue seizure orders.
e: Checkpoints are valid if limited to visual inspection; the plain view doctrine is one exception to the warrant requirement.
l: 1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 2; jurisprudence on plain view and checkpoints

q: An offense is punishable by imprisonment of five years. Is a preliminary investigation required before the information is filed?
a: Yes, because the penalty is at least four years, two months and one day
No, because preliminary investigation is required only for crimes punished by life imprisonment
No, because the penalty is below six years
Yes, but only if the accused requests it in writing
r: Rule 112, Section 1 requires preliminary investigation for offenses punishable by at least four years, two months and one day of imprisonment, regardless of the fine.
Preliminary investigation covers much more than crimes punished by life imprisonment.
The six-year line concerns the jurisdiction of first-level courts, not preliminary investigation.
Preliminary investigation is required by the Rules in these cases, not merely on request.
e: Preliminary investigation determines whether there is sufficient ground to believe a crime was committed and the respondent is probably guilty.

q: Two residents of the same barangay quarrel, and one files a criminal complaint for slight physical injuries directly with the court. What procedural defect is present?
a: The dispute should first have gone through barangay conciliation
The complaint should have been filed with the Sandiganbayan
The offended party should have filed a civil case instead
There is no defect, because criminal cases never need conciliation
r: Under the Katarungang Pambarangay law, disputes between residents of the same city or municipality involving offenses punishable by imprisonment not exceeding one year or a fine not exceeding P5,000 must first undergo conciliation.
The Sandiganbayan has nothing to do with this dispute.
The offended party may file a criminal case, but only after conciliation and a certification to file action.
Some criminal cases, those with light penalties, require conciliation first.
e: Barangay conciliation is a condition precedent; filing without it may lead to dismissal of the complaint.

q: Which distinction between preliminary investigation and inquest is correct?
a: Preliminary investigation is for respondents not under lawful arrest; inquest is for those arrested without a warrant
Preliminary investigation is conducted by trial judges; inquest is conducted by police investigators
Preliminary investigation decides guilt; inquest decides the penalty
Preliminary investigation is optional; inquest is never allowed
r: An inquest is a summary proceeding for persons lawfully arrested without a warrant; a preliminary investigation is a fuller inquiry where the respondent is not under detention.
Both are conducted by prosecutors.
Neither decides guilt or penalty; both concern probable cause.
Both are recognized procedures under the Rules.
e: A person arrested without a warrant may ask for a preliminary investigation, but must sign a waiver of Article 125 with the assistance of counsel.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 112, Secs. 1 and 6

q: A person was arrested without a warrant for a crime requiring preliminary investigation and wants one. What must he do?
a: Execute a waiver of Article 125 of the RPC with the assistance of counsel
Wait for the case to be filed and ask the court to dismiss it
Pay bail to the arresting officer at the station
Ask the barangay to conduct the preliminary investigation
r: Under Rule 112, Section 6, a person arrested without a warrant may ask for a preliminary investigation before the information is filed, but must sign a waiver of Article 125 in the presence of counsel.
He may also ask for a preliminary investigation within five days after learning that the case was filed, but a waiver is needed if he wants it before filing.
Bail is posted with the court, not paid to the arresting officer.
Barangay officials do not conduct preliminary investigations.
e: Article 125 sets the periods within which a person arrested without a warrant must be delivered to judicial authorities.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 112, Sec. 6; Revised Penal Code, Art. 125

q: Under Rule 114, in which situation is bail a matter of right?
a: Before conviction, for offenses not punishable by death, reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment
After conviction by the Regional Trial Court, for any offense charged in the information
Only for offenses committed by first-time offenders
Only when the accused can pay in cash
r: Rule 114, Section 4 makes bail a matter of right before conviction by the RTC for offenses not punishable by death, reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment, and before or after conviction by first-level courts.
After conviction by the RTC, bail becomes discretionary.
The right to bail does not depend on being a first-time offender.
Bail may be given as corporate surety, property bond, cash deposit or recognizance.
e: For offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment, bail is denied when evidence of guilt is strong, after a hearing.

q: An accused charged with murder applies for bail. What must the judge do before ruling?
a: Conduct a hearing to determine whether the evidence of guilt is strong
Grant bail automatically because the accused is presumed innocent
Deny bail automatically because murder is a heinous crime
Ask the prosecutor to fix the amount of bail without a hearing
r: For offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua, a bail hearing is required to determine whether the evidence of guilt is strong.
The presumption of innocence does not make bail automatic for such offenses.
Bail may be granted if the evidence of guilt is not strong.
The court, not the prosecutor, decides bail after a hearing.
e: Denying or granting bail in capital offenses without a hearing is grave abuse of discretion.

q: At arraignment, the accused refuses to enter any plea. What should the court do?
a: Enter a plea of not guilty for him
Enter a plea of guilty for him
Dismiss the case for lack of a plea
Postpone the case until the accused enters a plea
r: Rule 116, Section 1(c) provides that if the accused refuses to plead, a plea of not guilty shall be entered for him.
A plea of guilty must come from the accused himself.
Refusal to plead is not a ground for dismissal.
The Rules provide for a plea of not guilty instead of indefinite postponement.
e: A plea of not guilty is also entered when the accused makes a conditional plea or pleads guilty but presents exculpatory evidence.

q: After the prosecution rested its case, the defense believes the evidence is insufficient. What may the defense file?
a: A demurrer to evidence
A motion to quash the information
A petition for review with the DOJ
A motion for a bill of particulars
r: Rule 119, Section 23 allows the accused to file a demurrer to evidence after the prosecution rests, on the ground of insufficiency of evidence.
A motion to quash is filed before arraignment, against defects in the information.
A petition for review challenges the prosecutor's finding of probable cause, not the evidence at trial.
A bill of particulars is asked before arraignment to clarify vague allegations.
e: If a demurrer is filed without leave of court and is denied, the accused waives the right to present evidence.

q: A ten-year-old witness becomes frightened in the courtroom while testifying against her abuser. Which measure may the court allow under the Rule on Examination of a Child Witness?
a: Testimony through live-link television outside the courtroom
Postponement of her testimony until she turns eighteen
Replacing her testimony with the police report
Requiring her to testify only in written form
r: The Rule allows live-link television testimony, a support person, screens and other protective measures for child witnesses.
Delaying testimony until adulthood is not a measure under the Rule.
A police report cannot replace the child's testimony.
The Rule provides for oral testimony with protective measures, not written testimony only.
e: The Rule on Examination of a Child Witness aims to create an environment that allows the child to give reliable testimony without further trauma.
l: Rule on Examination of a Child Witness, A.M. No. 004-07-SC

q: During cross-examination, defense counsel asks the prosecution witness, 'You were drinking that night, weren't you?' The prosecutor objects that it is leading. How should the court rule?
a: Overrule the objection, because leading questions are allowed on cross-examination
Sustain the objection, because leading questions are never allowed
Sustain the objection, because cross-examination must be limited to new matters
Overrule the objection only if the witness is a child
r: Leading questions are allowed on cross-examination, which tests the accuracy and truthfulness of the witness.
Leading questions are generally not allowed on direct examination, but they are allowed on cross.
Cross-examination may cover matters stated on direct and matters connected with them, including credibility.
The rule allowing leading questions on cross does not depend on the witness being a child.
e: The order of examination is direct, cross, re-direct and re-cross.
